props.title: Husbands and Wives
props.initialSlug: Marriage crumbles for two NYC couples in crisis

sections.content: Husbands and Wives (1992) marks Woody Allen's most experimental and raw examination of relationship dysfunction, filmed in a pseudo-documentary style that feels brutally authentic. The handheld camera work by Carlo Di Palma creates an unsettling intimacy that perfectly matches the film's exploration of marital collapse. Released during Allen's highly publicized split from Mia Farrow (who stars in the film), it carries an uncomfortable meta-commentary that's impossible to ignore, similar to how Scenes from a Marriage (1973) drew from Ingmar Bergman's personal life.

sections.content: The film's structure, with its direct-to-camera interviews and documentary-style interruptions, creates a startling sense of voyeurism that influenced later works like Marriage Story (2019) and Blue Valentine (2010). The way it captures the slow unraveling of relationships - both through Judy Davis and Sydney Pollack's explosive separation and the quieter dissolution of Allen and Farrow's characters - set a new standard for depicting marital discord on screen.

What makes Husbands and Wives particularly powerful is its unflinching look at how partners rationalize their behavior. The film's exploration of infidelity, aging, and attraction to younger partners eerily foreshadowed Allen's own public scandal. This self-awareness creates layers of meaning similar to those found in 8½ (1963), where Fellini's personal life bleeds into his art. SUBHEAD: Impact on Modern Relationship Films

sections.content: The film's influence can be seen in contemporary works like Before Midnight (2013) and Force Majeure (2014), which similarly examine the complicated dynamics of long-term relationships. Allen's use of handheld cameras and natural dialogue created a template for authentic relationship stories that continues to influence filmmakers today.
